actions.justification: MANDATORY: Patient with severe COPD presenting with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum - respiratory assessment is the first priority to characterize the severity of the exacerbation including breath sounds, use of accessory muscles, and work of breathing.
MANDATORY: Comprehensive vital signs assessment required to establish baseline and detect hemodynamic compromise or signs of respiratory failure in this COPD exacerbation.
MANDATORY: Chest X-ray is essential to identify precipitating causes of COPD exacerbation (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema) and guide treatment decisions.

MANDATORY: ABG is critical in AECOPD to assess for hypercapnic respiratory failure (elevated PaCO2, acidemia), which will guide decision-making regarding NIV or intubation. Must be completed within 60 minutes.
Assess for altered mental status or somnolence which may indicate hypercapnic encephalopathy, a sign of impending respiratory failure requiring urgent NIV or intubation in AECOPD.
Short-acting bronchodilators (e.g., salbutamol/ipratropium nebulization) are first-line treatment for AECOPD to relieve bronchospasm and improve airflow obstruction.

Patient with severe COPD presenting with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum - blood cultures should be obtained to evaluate for infectious etiology (bacterial exacerbation) before initiating antibiotics.
Systemic corticosteroids are standard of care for COPD exacerbation, reducing inflammation, improving lung function, and shortening recovery time per GOLD guidelines.

Although SpO2 is 98%, controlled supplemental oxygen may be needed; however, in severe COPD, target SpO2 88-92% to avoid hypercapnic respiratory failure. Initiating controlled O2 therapy is appropriate during initial management of COPD exacerbation.

AECOPD with increased sputum production indicates likely infectious exacerbation. Antibiotics are recommended per GOLD guidelines when patients have increased sputum purulence, increased dyspnea, or increased sputum volume (Anthonisen criteria). This patient has at least 2 criteria (increased dyspnea, increased sputum).
CBC will help assess for leukocytosis suggesting infection, anemia, or other hematologic abnormalities contributing to dyspnea in this COPD exacerbation patient.

For severe COPD exacerbation, NIV (BiPAP) is a key intervention that reduces need for intubation and improves outcomes. Assessing eligibility is important even though current SpO2 is adequate, as the patient has severe COPD and may deteriorate.

BMP is indicated to assess electrolytes (especially potassium and bicarbonate which may be affected by bronchodilators and corticosteroids), renal function, and to complement ABG findings in this AECOPD patient.
Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral AECOPD exacerbations and can guide antibiotic stewardship decisions in this patient with severe COPD who has already received antibiotics.

Sputum culture is indicated in AECOPD with increased sputum production to identify causative pathogens and guide targeted antibiotic therapy, particularly important in severe COPD where resistant organisms may be present.
Lactate level helps assess metabolic status and severity of respiratory compromise in AECOPD, particularly to rule out tissue hypoxia or lactic acidosis from respiratory failure.
Pulmonology consultation is appropriate for severe COPD exacerbation to guide advanced management decisions including NIV optimization, ventilatory support, and disposition.
CT chest can identify complications of AECOPD such as pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, or pneumonia not visible on plain X-ray, which may be contributing to the worsening dyspnea.

Patient with severe COPD exacerbation presenting with worsening dyspnea may have reduced oral intake and increased insensible losses. Cautious IV fluid administration can support hydration, though must be balanced against risk of fluid overload in COPD patients. Vitals are currently stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%) so careful hydration is appropriate as a supportive measure.

Patient with severe COPD and worsening dyspnea may have a component of fluid overload contributing to respiratory distress. A diuretic can help reduce any pulmonary congestion. SpO2 is currently stable at 98%, and vitals are relatively stable, making this a reasonable optional intervention to consider while awaiting diagnostic results.
Only available action in current phase; patient is hemodynamically stable so clinical threshold for vasopressors not met, but system requires action selection from available list.
NIV eligibility was assessed; reassessment of response to current therapy and need for NIV initiation is warranted given severe COPD exacerbation and ongoing dyspnea.

Multiple labs are pending (CBC, blood culture, ABG, sputum culture, procalcitonin, lactate). Reviewing results as they return is critical to guide ongoing management of this COPD exacerbation, identify superimposed infection, and assess oxygenation/ventilation status.

Patient has received bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, and supplemental oxygen. A formal reassessment of respiratory response to these therapies is needed to determine if NIV escalation or further intervention is required.
